p.x:
When I was a child, I lived with my grandparents in a small village. I didn't have many toys, but I was very happy. My sister had one doll, and I had a ball. Every day after school, we played with the other children in the street.
My grandmother always gave us sweets on Sundays, and my grandfather told us funny stories. I remember the day my baby brother was born. He cried all the time, and I was a bit jealous!
When we were young, we didn't have a playground, but there was a big tree with a swing. In the windy season, we made kites from paper and flew them in the rice fields. I was sometimes naughty, and I was scared of the dark, but I loved my childhood. Now I live in Bangkok, but I still visit the village every year.

Ask your grandparents about their childhood, and you will probably hear very different stories from your own. Fifty years ago, most children in Thailand grew up in the countryside. They played outside all day, climbed trees, built treehouses and played hide and seek until it got dark. Toys were simple, and many children made their own.
Children also helped at home. Every child had chores, such as feeding the chickens or washing clothes. Pocket money was rare. Parents were often strict, and children were expected to be quiet and polite.
Today, many children grow up in cities. Toddlers go to nursery, and older children spend hours on homework and extra classes. Instead of crayons and paper, they draw on tablets, and they watch cartoons on YouTube rather than on TV once a week. Some parents spoil their children with expensive gifts, and a toddler's tantrum in a shopping mall is a common sight.
But some things never change. Children still love bedtime stories, and they are still full of curiosity about the world. And most adults, looking back, remember their childhood as a carefree time and have happy memories of it.

Psychologists have long argued that the experiences of early childhood are formative, shaping who we become as adults. The relationships children form, the way they are nurtured, and the opportunities they have to explore all leave lasting effects, many of which become clear only in adolescence or later.
One area that has attracted growing attention is play. Researchers distinguish between structured activities, such as music lessons or sports clubs, and unstructured play, in which children invent their own games without adult direction. Unstructured play, it seems, is especially valuable: it develops creativity, problem-solving and the ability to manage emotions. Yet in many societies it is disappearing. Busy schedules, concerns about safety and the attraction of screens mean that children spend far less time playing freely outdoors than previous generations did.
Some experts blame overprotective parenting. Out of understandable fear, parents may prevent children from taking small risks, such as climbing a tree or walking to school alone, which help them build confidence and independence. A mischievous adventure that ends in a scraped knee, they argue, can teach more than an afternoon of supervised activities.
It is also worth noting how memory shapes our view of the past. Adults often feel nostalgic about their early years, reminiscing about long summers and simple pleasures. These vivid recollections are not always accurate, but they reveal what we cherish. Perhaps the most important milestone of childhood is not learning to read or walk, but learning that the world is a place worth exploring.
